newsitem.title: PERU: Japan hopes hostage crisis talks to stay on course.
newsitem.headline: Japan hopes hostage crisis talks to stay on course.

text.p: Japanese officials said on Tuesday they hoped talks to end Peru's 14-day-old hostage crisis would stay on track despite unexpected access by journalists to the inside of the Japanese ambassador's residence.
"We hope this will not influence a peaceful resolution," a spokesman for the Japanese task force monitoring the crisis in Lima told reporters.

Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels allowed a group of local and foreign journalists to enter the captured official residence of Japanese ambasssador Morihisa Aoki for the first time on Tuesday.
The move took the task force by surprise, the spokesman said. "The situation is changing step by step. We have to brace ourselves because we don't know what is going to happen next," he said.
Televised reports by journalists contained detailed images of the Marxist guerrillas and some of their most valuable captives, including Aoki and Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela.

In a brief interview session a gaunt-looking Aoki apologised in Japanese for the embassy's involvement in the hostage crisis which began December 17 when about 20 Marxist rebels stormed his lavish cocktail party honouring Japanese Emperor Akihito's 63rd birthday.
He said the hostages had maintained a feeling of solidarity, and called for a swift, peaceful resolution to the crisis.
"It seems like Ambassador Aoki has gotten a little thin, but he still has high morale. He is assuming responsibility and showing deep consideration to everybody," the spokesman said.
Japan's 50-member diplomatic task force is led by Japan's ambassador to Mexico, Terusuke Terada, and composed of officials from Tokyo, Latin America and the United States.
Despite the crisis Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said earlier on Tuesday he would go ahead with a five-nation Asian tour starting on January 7 that officials had said might be cancelled.
"I place my entire trust in Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori and have made arrangements so I can always be contacted," Hashimoto told reporters in Tokyo.
